Annual Crop Land: Annual Crop Land shows rectangular or trapezoidal cultivated parcels with sharp, straight boundaries separating adjacent fields.
Annual Crop Land exhibits high contrast in color and texture between neighboring parcels due to differing crop types or growth stages.
Annual Crop Land contains large expanses of exposed bare soil visible as light brown or tan patches, especially during planting or fallow periods.
Annual Crop Land displays a fine-grained, uniform texture within each parcel, contrasting with the coarse, mottled texture of Forest.
Annual Crop Land lacks the repeated, evenly spaced circular or oval patterns of tree crowns seen in Permanent Crop Land.
Annual Crop Land features regularly spaced, parallel furrows or ridges aligned across entire parcels, unlike the irregular or absent micro-topography of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land has higher geometric regularity in parcel layout than Herbaceous Vegetation Land, which shows amorphous, diffuse vegetation patches.
Annual Crop Land shows abrupt transitions in surface reflectance at parcel edges, whereas Forest exhibits gradual canopy density gradients.
Annual Crop Land contains narrow, straight access roads dividing parcels into grids, unlike the meandering or sparse tracks in Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land presents dominant hues of green, brown, and ochre in close juxtaposition, lacking the deep, uniform dark green of mature Forest canopy.
Annual Crop Land parcels are typically smaller and more numerous than the expansive, contiguous grassy areas of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land lacks the dense, overlapping canopy shadows characteristic of Forest, instead showing high albedo from soil or low-stature crops.
Annual Crop Land displays linear irrigation ditches forming right-angle networks within parcels, absent in Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Annual Crop Land has minimal internal texture variation within a single parcel during early growth stages, unlike the speckled heterogeneity of scattered shrubs in Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Annual Crop Land parcels often align precisely with cardinal directions, reflecting mechanized cultivation, unlike the organic orientation of Pasture Land boundaries.
Annual Crop Land shows frequent presence of temporary field access tracks that terminate at parcel edges, unlike the continuous, through-going roads in urban land.
Annual Crop Land contains no standing water bodies larger than small irrigation ponds, distinguishing it from flooded rice paddies misclassified as other agricultural types.
Annual Crop Land exhibits seasonal shifts in dominant color—brown to green to yellow—within the same parcel, unlike the stable green-brown mix of Permanent Crop Land.
Annual Crop Land parcels have consistent internal tonal homogeneity, contrasting with the patchy, variable brightness of grazed Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land lacks the dendritic or sinuous river patterns cutting through natural vegetation, instead featuring straight-edged canals oriented orthogonally to parcel boundaries.
Forest: Forest is a land cover class characterized by large, irregularly shaped patches of vegetation that lack the geometric field boundaries seen in Annual Crop Land or Permanent Crop Land.
Forest appears as dark green in satellite imagery, contrasting with the lighter green or yellowish tones of Herbaceous Vegetation Land and Pasture Land.
Forest exhibits a coarse, mottled texture from overlapping tree crowns, unlike the smoother, more uniform texture of Pasture Land or Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Forest shows minimal internal linear segmentation, whereas Annual Crop Land displays frequent straight plow or harvest striping patterns.
Forest lacks the regularly spaced, parallel rows characteristic of Permanent Crop Land orchards or vineyards.
Forest contains few or no visible roads cutting through its interior, unlike Pasture Land which often has dense, branching farm road networks.
Forest features high canopy density with little to no exposed soil visible between trees, in contrast to the patchy soil exposure common in Annual Crop Land during planting or fallow periods.
Forest forms contiguous wooded areas spanning hundreds of meters without abrupt edges, unlike the small, discrete parcels typical of Permanent Crop Land.
Forest has irregular, dendritic river courses flowing through it, whereas rivers in Annual Crop Land often follow straight, canalized, or grid-aligned paths.
Forest displays variable crown shadowing due to vertical layering and height variation, unlike the low, even shadowing of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Forest lacks the rectangular, gridded parcel layout seen in many Pasture Land and Annual Crop Land regions.
Forest shows no evidence of irrigation ditches arranged in orthogonal grids, a feature commonly present in Permanent Crop Land and some Annual Crop Land.
Forest contains winding, narrow forest trails rather than the wide, straight access roads typical of large-scale crop fields.
Forest has complex, fractal-like patch edges with high perimeter-to-area ratios, unlike the simpler, convex shapes of many agricultural fields.
Forest exhibits muted color variation across its extent, lacking the seasonal color bands (e.g., alternating green/yellow/brown) seen in rotational Annual Crop Land.
Forest contains no visible hedgerows aligned in straight lines, distinguishing it from Pasture Land where such linear woody features are common boundary markers.
Forest shows no alignment of vegetation strips with cardinal directions, unlike the strongly oriented row crops in Permanent Crop Land.
Forest has low building density with structures rarely clustered or aligned, in contrast to the linear farmstead arrangements often found along field edges in Pasture Land.
Forest displays no visible center-pivot irrigation circles, a hallmark feature absent in natural forests but common in large-scale Annual Crop Land.
Forest contains no regularly spaced, evenly sized tree canopies indicative of plantation forestry, distinguishing it from managed Permanent Crop Land plantations.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land: Herbaceous Vegetation Land has irregular, organic patch boundaries that lack the straight, angular edges and sharp right-angle corners typical of Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows a fine, homogeneous grassy texture without the coarse, mottled, high-contrast canopy pattern characteristic of Forest.

Herbaceous Vegetation Land displays uniform medium-green reflectance with minimal color variation, unlike Permanent Crop Land which often exhibits alternating green-brown strips from bare soil or vine rows.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks visible plow lines, tillage marks, or parallel furrows that are consistently present in Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains no regularly spaced planting points, orchard grids, or linear trellis patterns seen in Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land features scattered, isolated trees with small crowns and no continuous woody canopy cover, distinguishing it from Forest’s dense, contiguous tree cover.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no evidence of paddock fencing, internal enclosure lines, or geometric subdivision into rectangular enclosures common in Pasture Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no row-crop geometry—such as evenly spaced parallel bands of vegetation and bare soil—that defines Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land exhibits soft, diffuse patch edges rather than the crisp, high-contrast field margins bounded by roads or ditches found in Pasture Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains no linear infrastructure such as orchard access roads aligned to planting grids, unlike Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has low structural heterogeneity: no vertical layering or shadowed understory texture visible in Forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the dark, elongated shadows cast by tall, regularly spaced tree canopies that appear in Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no evidence of irrigation ditches arranged in orthogonal or radial patterns, which frequently appear in irrigated Pasture Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no discernible crop residue patterns—like stubble fields or harvested swathes—that occur seasonally in Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land displays no road networks dividing land into uniform, rectilinear parcels as seen in intensively managed Pasture Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains no water bodies with engineered shorelines, canals, or geometric embankments typical of irrigated Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no clustered farmsteads, barns, or high-density rural building groups associated with intensive Pasture Land management.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no spectral contrast between adjacent fields due to different crop types or growth stages, a hallmark of Annual Crop Land mosaics.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the dense network of narrow, curvilinear tracks used for livestock movement that often crisscross Pasture Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land exhibits no abrupt transitions between vegetation and bare soil along straight lines—unlike the clean field-edge tillage boundaries defining Annual Crop Land.
Highway or Road: Highway or Road is a narrow, elongated corridor with uniform width over long distances, unlike rivers which exhibit variable width and meandering edges.
Highway or Road appears as a continuous linear feature connecting intersections and branching junctions, whereas residential buildings form compact, irregular clusters without such connectivity.
Highway or Road displays smooth, homogeneous surface texture with minimal internal variation, in contrast to industrial buildings which show heterogeneous rooftop patterns and structural complexity.
Highway or Road occupies a thin linear footprint rather than an area-filling patch, distinguishing it from herbaceous vegetation land that covers broad, contiguous parcels.
Highway or Road maintains geometric straightness or consistent curvature over extended segments, unlike rivers whose sinuosity creates frequent directional shifts.
Highway or Road lacks the dense, high-contrast texture of building rooftops, appearing instead as a low-contrast, uniformly toned band against surrounding land.
Highway or Road shows sharp, well-defined parallel edges throughout its length, whereas rivers have diffuse, irregular, and often vegetated margins.
Highway or Road forms a single dominant linear axis without internal subdivisions, unlike residential areas which contain intersecting street grids and fragmented lots.
Highway or Road exhibits consistent alignment across scene boundaries, while herbaceous vegetation land shows patchy, discontinuous coverage with irregular margins.
Highway or Road has no visible water presence, distinguishing it clearly from rivers which display specular reflection or dark blue-gray spectral signatures.
Highway or Road lacks the clustered, rectangular footprints characteristic of industrial buildings, instead presenting as a solitary, unbroken line.
Highway or Road appears darker and smoother than adjacent herbaceous vegetation land, which shows higher brightness and granular texture from plant canopies.
Highway or Road runs continuously through built-up areas without terminating abruptly, unlike residential building clusters which end at property lines or green buffers.
Highway or Road shows no evidence of roof structures, windows, or architectural detail, setting it apart from both residential and industrial buildings.
Highway or Road maintains constant orientation over kilometers, whereas rivers frequently change direction due to topographic constraints.
Highway or Road is flanked by narrow, linear roadside strips but remains itself a thin central corridor, unlike residential areas where development fills entire blocks.
Highway or Road displays minimal shadow variation along its length, indicating flat, even elevation, unlike industrial buildings which cast complex, overlapping shadows.
Highway or Road lacks the speckled brightness variation caused by scattered trees or shrubs, unlike herbaceous vegetation land which shows mottled reflectance.
Highway or Road exhibits high edge contrast against adjacent land cover types, while rivers often blend gradually into floodplains or riparian vegetation.
Highway or Road shows no branching into dense networks of smaller paths, distinguishing it from residential street grids that radiate from central nodes.
Industrial Buildings: Industrial Buildings have very large rectangular roof footprints that dominate the scene, unlike the smaller, irregularly shaped roofs of Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings appear in clusters of identical or near-identical large-volume structures, whereas Annual Crop Land shows repetitive linear rows of vegetation.
Industrial Buildings occupy broad paved yards and loading areas with minimal vegetation, contrasting sharply with the dense, continuous canopy cover of Permanent Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings are spaced farther apart on large individual parcels, unlike the high-density, small-footprint clustering of Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings feature extensive flat, uniform gray or metallic roof surfaces with sharp geometric edges, unlike the varied roof colors and textures of Residential Buildings.

Industrial Buildings are adjacent to wide access roads but retain dominant building mass coverage, whereas Highway or Road class is defined almost entirely by linear transport corridors with negligible building presence.
Industrial Buildings lack the fine-scale grid pattern of orchard rows seen in Permanent Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings show no evidence of seasonal crop row alignment or soil exposure between plants, distinguishing them from Annual Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings exhibit high roof-area-to-land-area ratios, exceeding those typical of Residential Buildings on comparable parcel sizes.
Industrial Buildings often include large open storage surfaces with uniform albedo and no vegetation, unlike the heterogeneous ground cover of Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings display straight, parallel roof edges aligned across multiple structures, a level of geometric regularity absent in the organic layout of Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings have minimal tree cover or landscaped green space within their immediate footprint, unlike the frequent small yards and street trees associated with Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings feature long, uninterrupted rooflines exceeding 100 meters in length, far surpassing the typical roof lengths of Residential Buildings.

Industrial Buildings are surrounded by expansive asphalt or concrete surfaces with few or no parked vehicles visible, distinguishing them from the vehicle-dense parking lots often adjacent to but not integral to Highway or Road.
Industrial Buildings lack the curvilinear street networks and block-level subdivision patterns characteristic of Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings show no field-scale texture variation caused by windrows, irrigation furrows, or harvest marks found in Annual Crop Land.

Industrial Buildings have roof materials that reflect sunlight uniformly, producing consistent brightness values across large contiguous areas, unlike the speckled brightness of crop canopies in Permanent Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings contain no water bodies or drainage channels within their primary built footprint, unlike some low-lying Residential Building developments near wetlands.
Industrial Buildings exhibit high spatial separation between structures—often over 50 meters—whereas Residential Buildings typically abut or share walls in multi-unit configurations.
Industrial Buildings lack the fine-grained texture of tilled soil or emerging crop stands visible in early-season Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land: Pasture Land is a land parcel with irregular to moderately regular shapes that lack the tight geometric precision of Annual Crop Land fields.
Pasture Land shows uniformly fine-grained grassy texture without the strong linear row patterns visible in Permanent Crop Land.
Pasture Land appears as open, contiguous grassy areas without the seasonal bare-soil patches characteristic of Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land has smoother, more homogeneous vegetation cover than the patchy, uneven density typical of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land lacks the dense, closed canopy and dendritic shadow patterns of Forest.
Pasture Land exhibits clear, well-defined field boundaries unlike the diffuse or natural ecotone edges often seen in Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land displays minimal internal linear features such as irrigation ditches or planting furrows compared to Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land has low vegetation height and density, resulting in uniform brightness and minimal cast shadows unlike Forest.
Pasture Land parcels rarely contain orchard-scale tree rows or vineyard trellis alignments found in Permanent Crop Land.
Pasture Land shows no evidence of repeated parallel cultivation lines or plowed striping common in Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land typically contains no built structures or infrastructure denser than occasional isolated farm buildings, unlike intensively managed crop zones.
Pasture Land has soft-edged, gently undulating terrain expression in vegetation tone, contrasting with the sharp tonal transitions of recently tilled Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land lacks the high-contrast geometric repetition of tree canopies seen in orchards or plantations classified as Permanent Crop Land.
Pasture Land shows consistent medium-green spectral reflectance without the seasonal color cycling between green and brown typical of Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land contains no visible water bodies larger than incidental drainage ponds, distinguishing it from flooded rice paddies or aquaculture classified under other agricultural types.
Pasture Land has no discernible road network density or grid alignment within the parcel, unlike peri-urban or intensively farmed zones.
Pasture Land displays uniform grass coverage across slopes and gentle contours, whereas Herbaceous Vegetation Land often shows erosion-driven texture breaks and natural vegetation clumping.
Pasture Land parcels are generally larger and less subdivided than the small, densely packed plots typical of Permanent Crop Land.
Pasture Land lacks the fine-scale texture variation caused by mixed herbaceous species and woody regrowth seen in unmanaged Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land shows no evidence of harvesting machinery tracks or recent harvest residue patterns that appear in Annual Crop Land after cutting or threshing.
Permanent Crop Land: Permanent Crop Land shows regularly spaced dot-like tree or vine canopies arranged in precise rows or grids across the field.
Permanent Crop Land exhibits alternating banded texture from parallel strips of vegetation and bare soil or low grass between planted rows.
Permanent Crop Land displays linear canopy alignments that persist uniformly across the entire field parcel, unlike the patchy or shifting patterns in Annual Crop Land.
Permanent Crop Land has discrete, isolated woody canopy elements visible as repeating dots or short dashes, contrasting with the continuous green mass of Forest.
Permanent Crop Land features row-parallel linear gaps in vegetation cover that are narrower and more evenly spaced than the irregular bare patches in Pasture Land.

Permanent Crop Land contains geometrically regular rectangular or trapezoidal field parcels defined by consistent internal row orientation, unlike the amorphous shapes often seen in Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Permanent Crop Land shows high-contrast texture due to sharp transitions between dark green canopy rows and light-toned inter-row soil, absent in the low-contrast uniformity of Annual Crop Land.
Permanent Crop Land presents a fine-grained, repetitive texture at medium resolution, whereas Forest shows coarse, mottled, or clumpy canopy texture.
Permanent Crop Land includes straight, parallel canopy lines extending over hundreds of meters without curvature, unlike the meandering or clustered patterns in natural shrubland.
Permanent Crop Land reveals consistent row spacing intervals of 3–8 meters visible as periodic dark-green stripes, distinct from the variable or absent spacing in Pasture Land.
Permanent Crop Land displays canopy elements aligned along cardinal-direction axes with minimal angular deviation, unlike the organic orientation of tree clusters in secondary forest.
Permanent Crop Land has field boundaries that enclose plots with internal linear structure, whereas Herbaceous Vegetation Land typically lacks such internal geometric organization.
Permanent Crop Land shows inter-row zones with uniform brightness and low texture, indicating maintained ground cover or bare soil, unlike the heterogeneous, tussocky ground of Pasture Land.
Permanent Crop Land exhibits canopy rows oriented perpendicular to access roads, forming right-angle intersections visible across multiple adjacent fields.
Permanent Crop Land contains no visible seasonal crop residue or tillage patterns within rows, distinguishing it from recently harvested Annual Crop Land.
Permanent Crop Land maintains consistent row geometry across slope gradients, while Annual Crop Land often shows terracing or contour-following patterns that break straight-line continuity.
Permanent Crop Land features canopy rows that terminate cleanly at field edges without tapering or thinning, unlike the gradual density decline seen at forest margins.
Permanent Crop Land shows minimal shadow elongation between rows during midday, indicating low vertical canopy variation compared to the multi-layered height structure of Forest.
Permanent Crop Land has inter-row spaces wide enough to resolve as distinct light-toned bands at 10m resolution, unlike the sub-pixel gaps in dense orchards misclassified as Forest.
Permanent Crop Land displays uniform row direction across contiguous parcels separated by roads or ditches, indicating planned large-scale layout absent in fragmented Pasture Land.
Residential Buildings: Residential Buildings are characterized by clusters of small to medium-sized roof footprints arranged in irregular but locally connected groups rather than the isolated massive structures typical of Industrial Buildings.

Residential Buildings show a fine-grained texture composed of alternating patches of rooftops, small vegetated yards, and scattered trees, unlike the coarse, uniform expanses of paved lots in Industrial Buildings.

Residential Buildings feature local street networks with frequent branching, cul-de-sacs, and right-angle intersections forming compact neighborhood blocks, whereas Highway or Road appears as a single dominant linear corridor with minimal branching.

Residential Buildings occupy irregularly shaped patches that conform to natural terrain or historical property boundaries, unlike the large rectangular or parallelogram-shaped parcels typical of Annual Crop Land.

Residential Buildings exhibit moderate building density—neither sparse like rural housing nor continuous like urban high-rises—creating a mosaic pattern distinct from the low-density uniformity of Permanent Crop Land.
Residential Buildings display roofs in varied colors including gray, red, brown, and blue, producing chromatic heterogeneity absent in the monotonous green or brown tones of Annual Crop Land.

Residential Buildings contain narrow, low-contrast roads that meander through neighborhoods and terminate in cul-de-sacs, contrasting with the wide, high-contrast, straight-through highways of Highway or Road.

Residential Buildings have building footprints that are predominantly rectangular or L-shaped with consistent scale under 500 m², unlike the sprawling, irregular, and often warehouse-scale footprints of Industrial Buildings.

Residential Buildings include small, irregularly shaped vegetated areas interspersed among buildings, whereas Permanent Crop Land shows large, contiguous, geometrically precise tree canopies aligned in rows.
Residential Buildings lack the long, parallel, evenly spaced linear features characteristic of Annual Crop Land’s cultivated rows.
Residential Buildings show no large open water bodies or linear rivers cutting across the patch, distinguishing them from water-adjacent land-use classes not in the sibling list but visually salient.

Residential Buildings contain driveways and sidewalks as thin linear features branching from streets to individual buildings, unlike the absence of such micro-linear infrastructure in Annual Crop Land.

Residential Buildings have building orientations that vary slightly block-to-block due to street curvature and lot geometry, whereas Industrial Buildings often align uniformly along a single axis for logistical efficiency.

Residential Buildings display a moderate ratio of impervious surface to vegetation—higher than Permanent Crop Land but lower than Industrial Buildings—visible as a balanced mix of rooftops and green space.
Residential Buildings feature small, detached structures with visible setbacks from roads and neighbors, unlike the abutting, wall-to-wall construction common in dense Industrial Buildings.

Residential Buildings contain backyard spaces that are typically smaller than 200 m² and irregularly shaped, contrasting with the vast, empty, geometrically regular paved yards of Industrial Buildings.
Residential Buildings show evidence of mature, non-uniform tree canopy cover distributed across yards and streets, unlike the sparse or absent tree cover in Highway or Road.
Residential Buildings lack the large, uninterrupted rectangular fields bounded by straight hedgerows or irrigation ditches seen in Permanent Crop Land.

Residential Buildings have street widths typically under 12 meters with intermittent parking lanes, whereas Highway or Road exceeds 20 meters in width and lacks adjacent parking or frontage development.

Residential Buildings contain rooftop shapes with multiple gables, dormers, or asymmetrical slopes, creating higher edge density than the flat or gently sloped, monolithic roofs of Industrial Buildings.
River: River is a long, narrow, elongated linear feature that traverses the scene rather than forming a broad enclosed basin like a lake or sea.
River has a sinuous or meandering channel pattern with visible bends, unlike the straight or gently curved engineered alignment of highways or roads.
River exhibits branching tributary connections that converge into a main channel, distinguishing it from isolated linear roads or uniform forest edges.
River width varies gradually along its course, whereas highways and roads maintain relatively uniform engineered widths.
River banks are irregular and natural in outline, contrasting with the sharp, straight, paved margins of highways or roads.
River is bordered by thin, discontinuous strips of riparian vegetation that follow its curving course, unlike the dense, continuous canopy of forest.
River appears as a continuous, unbroken water-filled channel across varied terrain, unlike fragmented or patchy water bodies such as small ponds or reservoirs.
River displays subtle tonal variation along its length due to changes in depth, sediment load, or sun glint, unlike the uniform gray or asphalt tone of roads.
River often flows through low-lying topography with gentle gradients, visible as subtle elevation-related context, unlike roads which frequently traverse ridges or cut across slopes.
River has no parallel linear features at consistent spacing like road lanes or shoulder markings.
River lacks the geometric grid or hierarchical branching patterns typical of road networks.
River shows no evidence of artificial embankments, bridges, or overpasses visible as structural interruptions along its length.
River surface reflects sky light with variable intensity depending on local orientation and wind roughness, unlike the matte or specular but static reflectance of paved roads.
River occupies a central position within a natural drainage network, not terminating abruptly or ending at intersections like roads.
River is flanked by floodplain landforms—such as braided channels, oxbow lakes, or alluvial deposits—that are absent beside highways and roads.
River appears darker and more fluid in tone than the bright, high-contrast linear features of snow-covered or dry riverbeds, which are not water.
River maintains continuity across diverse land covers—including forest, cropland, and urban fringe—whereas roads often terminate or change character at land-cover boundaries.
River lacks the rectilinear segmentation and right-angle junctions characteristic of road intersections.
River exhibits fine-scale texture variation along its banks due to emergent vegetation, sediment bars, or shallow riffles, unlike the smooth, homogeneous edge of a highway.
River is consistently associated with upstream narrowing and downstream widening in its channel morphology, unlike the uniform cross-section of engineered roads.
Sea or Lake: Sea or Lake is a large, contiguous expanse of water occupying a dominant portion of the scene with no visible segmentation by landforms.
Sea or Lake is a broad open-water area whose width exceeds its length by a factor of at least three, unlike the narrow linear form of a river.
Sea or Lake has a compact, rounded, lobed, or irregular shoreline boundary enclosing water, rather than the thin, meandering, branching pattern typical of rivers.
Sea or Lake shows uninterrupted water surface interior with no visible bars, sandbanks, or frequent land crossings that divide the water body.
Sea or Lake displays a high water-surface area-to-perimeter ratio, indicating enclosure by shoreline rather than elongation along a channel.
Sea or Lake exhibits uniform blue or blue-gray spectral signature across its entire visible extent without abrupt color breaks or vegetation intrusions.
Sea or Lake lacks the fine-scale linear texture of herbaceous vegetation land, appearing instead as a smooth, homogeneous water surface.
Sea or Lake contains no discernible field boundaries, crop rows, or geometric agricultural patterns that characterize herbaceous vegetation land.
Sea or Lake shows no evidence of pasture fencing, grazing tracks, or patchy green-brown mosaics typical of pasture land.
Sea or Lake has no visible road networks, built infrastructure, or human-made linear features crossing or bordering its water surface.
Sea or Lake occupies a topographically low-lying basin or coastal indentation, contrasting with the elevated or linear corridor position of rivers.
Sea or Lake presents a continuous water reflectance signature without the speckled or dappled brightness variation seen in shallow or turbid rivers.
Sea or Lake lacks the dense, fine-grained green texture of herbaceous vegetation land and instead shows uniform water reflectance.
Sea or Lake has no visible riparian vegetation corridors flanking its edges, unlike rivers which commonly display linear green bands along banks.
Sea or Lake displays minimal shoreline vegetation encroachment, with sharp water-land transitions rather than gradual green fringes typical of pasture land.
Sea or Lake shows no evidence of livestock clustering, paddock divisions, or rotational grazing patterns visible as geometric green-brown patches.
Sea or Lake exhibits specular reflection highlights over large areas under sunlight, unlike the subdued or fragmented glint of narrow river segments.
Sea or Lake has no visible sediment plumes, turbidity gradients, or sinuous flow-direction indicators that distinguish active rivers.
Sea or Lake maintains consistent water color and tone across its full extent, without the variable brown-green hue shifts common in shallow rivers or flooded pastures.
Sea or Lake appears as a single dominant water mass with no branching tributaries or distributary channels radiating from it, unlike river networks.
